items.title: Andy Reid’s legendary secret mac-n-cheese recipe has finally been shared with the world
items.summary:
Family, friends, football – Turkey Day is many things, but food is always at the center. Making the best side dish for Thanksgiving can occasionally feel like playing against the clock. Do you know how to make it exactly like grandma did? How are you supposed to keep it at optimum serving temperature when the turkey still has an hour to go? And most importantly, will the final product get the approval of that one aunt who never seems to like anything? 

No playbook, however, has been as fiercely guarded as NFL coach Andy Reid’s secret recipe for mac-and-cheese . For years, football fans whispered about the Kansas City Chiefs coach’s legendary cheesy creation. Whenever reporters asked for details, he stayed notoriously tight-lipped. Could anyone make him give up his culinary game plan ?

Players, coaches, even The Washington Post tried to crack the case . Now, journalist Pablo Torre has finally uncovered the full recipe.

The tasty mystery behind the mac-and-cheese 

This cheesy journey began at an airport terminal in 2018. Writer Charles McDonald bumped into Reid , and the conversation turned to Thanksgiving food.

McDonald says that Reid pulled up various recipes on his phone. Then the famous coach offhandedly mentioned that his creamy version of the pasta classic features seven different cheeses. In the video, he only lists six cheeses: fontina, mozzarella, parmesan, sharp cheddar, gouda, and gruyere. The mystery of the seventh cheese left fans obsessed with tracking down the final ingredient. 

Why football fans craved Coach Reid’s recipe 

Andy Reid is famous for much…
items.t: Andy Reid’s legendary secret mac-n-cheese recipe has finally been shared with the world

items.title: Taylor Swift surprises 81-year-old Brenda Lee with RIAA Diamond plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.’
items.summary:
Holiday season energy is officially here. Soon, the sounds of sleigh bells and Ho-ho-hoing Santas will fill every shopping center you walk into . And chances are good that you’ll hear the festive “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree” pumping out of the mall’s speakers at least once. The singer, Brenda Lee, was only a tween when she recorded the perennial classic. 

Decades later, the song continues to climb the charts every December. Now it has earned a massive RIAA Diamond certification for surpassing 10 million copies . To mark the historic milestone, music superstar Taylor Swift surprised the 81-year-old legend in person. The heartwarming meetup brought Lee to tears. 

A heartfelt surprise between two music icons 

Seeing Taylor Swift present a gleaming Diamond plaque to Brenda Lee on behalf of the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) is a true gift to music fans. The song is an enduring holiday classic for sure, but there are even deeper connections between Swift and Lee. They both started young and began their recording careers in Tennessee. Swift’s debut album arrived when she turned 16 , while Lee was only 12. 

There’s plenty about this musician meet-cute that will bring a smile to your face. Especially Lee’s adorable astonishment at Taylor Swift’s height. When wearing heels, Swift is six feet tall. 

But the real emotion comes after Brenda Lee receives the Diamond Certification. She tears up as she mentions the song’s writer, Johnny Marks . You probably know his two other seasonal classics, “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” and “A Holly Jolly Christmas.”…
items.t: Taylor Swift surprises 81-year-old Brenda Lee with RIAA Diamond plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.’

items.title: The origin of the Thanksgiving holiday actually had nothing to do with the Pilgrims or Native Americans
items.summary:
For many decades, Americans have debated Thanksgiving and the “first Thanksgiving” story, digging into the history versus the mythology of the Pilgrims and Native Americans breaking bread together. Some even shun the holiday to protest how the Thanksgiving origin story has been sanitized to obscure painful historical realities.

The problem is that that hotly debated history is a myth within another myth, as the federal Thanksgiving holiday wasn’t originally tied to the Pilgrims, Native Americans, or Plymouth at all. 

Let’s unpack it. 

The first presidential Thanksgiving proclamation had zero mention of the Pilgrims 

Local Thanksgiving festivals had been observed in the U.S. long before it became a national holiday, often to give thanks for a successful harvest. But the official holiday is an entirely different thing. 

The first federal U.S. Thanksgiving holiday was proclaimed by George Washington in October of 1789 (which you can read here ). None of its over 450 words mention, or even allude to, the Pilgrims sitting down to feast with the Wampanoag people. 

Instead, Washington declared Thursday, November 26th, a holiday to give “sincere and humble thanks” to “that great and glorious Being, who is the beneficent Author of all the good that was, that is, or that will be” for bounties including the outcome of the Revolutionary War, the establishment of a constitutional government, the “civil and religious liberty with which we are blessed,” the ability to acquire knowledge, and the general blessings and favors of God. He also called for prayers asking God to pardon…
items.t: The origin of the Thanksgiving holiday actually had nothing to do with the Pilgrims or Native Americans

items.title: Tattoos have become as American as apple pie. But it turns out they still make people nervous.
items.summary:
If you went back in time to the 1980s , one of the biggest changes you’d notice is the lack of tattoos. It’s estimated that in the ’80s, around 10% of the American population was tatted, as compared to 32% today. Public opinion began to shift in the 1990s as alternative and punk rock subcultures hit the mainstream and even straight-laced folks started getting inked.

In the ‘90s, tattoos shifted from a symbol of gangs, the military, or dangerous subcultures to an art form, with the rise of superstar tattoo artists such as Ed Hardy and Mr. Cartoon . Another big cultural shift during this time was that women made up a large number of those embracing the new body aesthetic. 

Tattoos have reached the mainstream, and visible ink is now acceptable in many professions where it used to be forbidden, so these days, body art doesn’t seem intimidating. However, a new study by Farid Pazhoohi, Ph.D., published in Evolutionary Psychological Science found that tattoos still make people a little uncomfortable.

Why We Might Give Tattooed Strangers a Little More Room | Farid Pazhoohi Ph D, Psychology Today

items.t: Tattoos have become as American as apple pie. But it turns out they still make people nervous.

items.title: Neil Diamond wrote The Monkees’ biggest hit, but they weren’t his first choice to sing it
items.summary:
Sixty years ago, The Monkees released “I’m a Believer,” which became the group’s biggest hit, spending a remarkable seven consecutive weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100.

And of course, musical talent aside, the band certainly had Neil Diamond to thank, since he wrote the song. Only Diamond originally envisioned a much different singer to bring the song to life. 

“I’m a Believer”…as a country song? 

In 1966, Diamond was in New York, on the precipice of a breakthrough as a solo songwriter, following the success of his single “Cherry, Cherry .” During this time, Diamond wrote “I’m a Believer,” which he considered for country music crooner Eddy Arnold, known for “Make the World Go Away.”

Not exactly the upbeat, radio-friendly pop group The Monkees would become.

However, music executive Don Kirshner steered the song to The Monkees instead, with Micky Dolenz singing lead vocals and Jeff Barry as the producer.

And the timing of that decision couldn’t have worked out any better. When “I’m a Believer” was released, the Monkees’ self-titled sitcom premiered on NBC, and their debut single, “Last Train to Clarksville,” had reached No. 1 on the Hot 100.

The Monkees had a pretty incredible run with it 

“I’m a Believer” quickly became one of the defining songs of the decade and helped establish The Monkees as something much bigger than a fictional band created for television. Not to mention, it became one of Diamond’s most celebrated songwriting achievements. A win-win all around. 

But the song’s story didn’t end with the 1960s. Diamond eventually recorded his own version in 1971,…
items.t: Neil Diamond wrote The Monkees’ biggest hit, but they weren’t his first choice to sing it

items.title: Vet demonstrates ‘squish the cat’ method of safe cat handling in delightfully helpful video
items.summary:
If you’ve ever tried to make a cat do something it doesn’t want to do, you’ve likely experienced the terror that a cat’s wrath can invoke. Our cute, cuddly feline friends may be small, but the razor blades on their feet are no joke when they decide to utilize them. Even cats who love us can get spicy if we try to manhandle them , so we can imagine how things will go with cats who don’t know us well. But sometimes it’s necessary to handle a cat even if it’s resistant to the idea.

This is where Vancouver veterinarian Dr. Uri Burstyn comes in. His “How to pick up a cat like a pro” video , in which he demonstrates a few ways of picking up and handling a cat, has been viewed over 23 million times since he shared it in 2018. Unlike many viral videos, it’s not humorous and nothing outrageous happens, but the combo of Burstyn’s calm demeanor and his repeated instructions to “squish that cat” has endeared him to the masses .

The video truly is helpful; he shows the ways to pick up a cat that make them feel the most secure using his cats, Claudia (then 1 year old) and Mr. Pirate (then 14). He explains that cats spook very easily and it’s best to introduce yourself to them gently. Let them sniff your fingers, keeping your fingers curled in, and once they’ve sniffed you, you can often give them a light rub on the cheek or under the chin.

Picking them up is a different story. The reason many cats will claw or scratch you when you try to pick them up is because they feel unsupported or unsafe , so they’ll scramble around trying to get some…
items.t: Vet demonstrates ‘squish the cat’ method of safe cat handling in delightfully helpful video

Kaeden Henry, then a sixth grader living in Florida, bravely pondered a question few (if any) have been brave enough to ask: do cat buttholes touch every surface they sit on?

items.title: A juice company dumped orange peels in a national park. This is what it looks like today.
items.summary:
In 1997, ecologists Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs approached an orange juice company in Costa Rica called Del Oro with an off-the-wall idea . In exchange for donating a portion of unspoiled, forested land to the Área de Conservación Guanacaste, a nature preserve in the country’s northwest, the park would allow the company to dump its discarded orange peels and pulp, free of charge, in a heavily grazed, largely deforested area nearby.

One year later, one thousand trucks poured into the national park, offloading over 12,000 metric tons of sticky, mealy, orange compost onto the worn-out plot. The project was forced to end after just its second year, though, when rival juice manufacturer TicoFrut sued Del Oro, alleging it had defiled a national park, and Costa Rica’s Supreme Court ultimately sided with the plaintiff. The site was left untouched and largely unexamined for over a decade.

Finding the site years later on 

Sixteen years later, Janzen dispatched graduate student Timothy Treuer to look for the site where the food waste was dumped.

Treuer initially set out to locate the large placard that marked the plot, and failed.

The first deposit of orange peels in 1997. Photo by Dan Janzen. 

“It’s a huge sign, bright yellow lettering. We should have been able to see it,” Treuer says. After wandering around for half an hour with no luck, he consulted Janzen, who gave him more detailed instructions on how to find the plot.

When he returned a week later and confirmed he was in the right place, Treuer was floored. Compared to the adjacent barren former pastureland, the…
items.t: A juice company dumped orange peels in a national park. This is what it looks like today.

items.title: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
items.summary:
A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. 

“As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” 

Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) 

The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung 
 Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. 

“Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning,…
items.t: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
